headings.title: Introduction to Cancer and Pathophysiology
headings.content: Cancer begins at the cellular level when genetic mutations disrupt normal cell division and growth. Instead of following the orderly cycle of growth, division, and programmed cell death, mutated cells multiply uncontrollably. These abnormal cells form masses known as neoplasms or tumors. Tumors can be **benign**, meaning they remain localized and do not spread to other tissues, or **malignant**, meaning they invade surrounding structures and can metastasize to distant organs through the blood or lymphatic systems.

headings.title: Common Types and Classifications of Cancer
headings.content:
- **Carcinomas**: Tumors originating in epithelial tissues, which line the body surfaces, cavities, and organs. Examples include breast, lung, and cervical cancers.
- **Sarcomas**: Cancers arising from connective or supportive tissues such as bones, muscles, fat, and blood vessels.
- **Leukemias**: Malignancies of the blood-forming tissues, characterized by the overproduction of abnormal white blood cells in the bone marrow.
- **Lymphomas and Myelomas**: Cancers affecting the immune system, specifically involving lymphocytes and plasma cells.

headings.title: Etiology and Risk Factors in the Nigerian Context
headings.content:
Cancer etiology involves a complex interaction of genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors. In Nigeria, certain infectious agents contribute significantly to the cancer burden. 

1. **Infectious Agents**: Persistent infections such as Human Papillomavirus are major drivers of cervical cancer, while Hepatitis B and C viruses strongly correlate with hepatocellular carcinoma.
2. **Lifestyle and Environmental Exposures**: Tobacco use, heavy alcohol consumption, and dietary habits low in fiber increase risk. Additionally, indoor air pollution from biomass fuel smoke and occupational exposures pose distinct challenges.
3. **Genetics**: Inherited gene mutations, such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, elevate susceptibility to specific breast and ovarian malignancies.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Early Warning Signs
headings.content: Cancer can present with diverse symptoms depending on its location and stage. Nurses must remain vigilant for systemic indicators such as unexplained weight loss, persistent fatigue, and recurrent fevers. Localized signs often include palpable lumps, persistent cough, changes in bowel habits, or unusual bleeding. Recognizing these early warning signs prompts timely medical evaluation, which is vital for improving overall treatment outcomes.

headings.title: Diagnostic Procedures and Staging
headings.content:
Accurate diagnosis and staging dictate the management plan for any cancer patient. Screening tools and diagnostic workups typically combine laboratory assays, imaging studies, and definitive tissue biopsy. 

| Diagnostic Method | Primary Purpose |
|---|---| 
| Imaging (X-ray, CT, MRI) | Visualizing tumor location and size |
| Biopsy | Providing definitive microscopic confirmation of malignancy |
| Tumor Markers | Detecting specific proteins shed by cancer cells in blood |

Staging systems, such as the TNM system (Tumor, Node, Metastasis), describe the anatomical extent of the disease to guide therapy choices.

headings.title: Medical and Surgical Treatments
headings.content: Treatment modalities depend on cancer type, stage, and the patient's overall health status. Surgery aims to physically remove localized tumors and surrounding margins. Medical therapies include **chemotherapy**, which uses cytotoxic drugs to destroy rapidly dividing cells, and **radiation therapy**, which utilizes high-energy rays to damage cancer cell DNA. Targeted therapies and immunotherapy are newer approaches that focus on specific molecular targets or boost the body's natural defenses against malignant cells.

headings.title: Home Healthcare Nursing Management for Cancer Patients
headings.content: Managing cancer care within the home setting requires comprehensive support for both the patient and their family caregivers. Nurses play a crucial role in managing side effects such as nausea, fatigue, and pain arising from treatments. Education regarding medication administration, infection prevention strategies due to treatment-induced immunosuppression, and nutritional support is vital. Regular home visits allow nurses to monitor complications early and provide necessary psychological encouragement.

headings.title: Palliative Care and End-of-Life Support
headings.content: Palliative care focuses on improving the quality of life for patients facing life-limiting illnesses through symptom relief, pain management, and holistic support. Unlike curative treatment, palliative interventions can be integrated at any stage of a serious illness alongside active therapies. When a cure is no longer possible, end-of-life care ensures dignity, comfort, and emotional and spiritual support for the patient and their loved ones.
